# Overview

This document accompanies "Missing not at Random Analyses for Multilevel
Data" and describes the equivalence between the dummy-coded missingness
models used in the paper and the item response theory (IRT) missingness
models of Cursio et al. (2019). The GitHub repository at
[https://github.com/blimp-stats/mnar-mlm](https://github.com/blimp-stats/mnar-mlm)
includes the paper, the example data sets, and the `rblimp` script
(`rblimp/irt-missingness-models.R`) that fits the models shown here.

Dummy coding is equivalent to the one- and two-parameter IRT missingness
models in Cursio et al. (2019). Their framework uses a standardized
latent variable to represent person-level missingness propensity and a
measurement model with the *T* binary missing data indicators as the
"items." After removing all group effects, the dummy-coded model is
fully equivalent to a one-parameter IRT model. With group effects
included, the dummy-coded model is analogous to a multiple-group IRT
model that imposes metric invariance (common factor loadings or
discrimination parameters) while allowing scalar noninvariance
(group-specific intercepts or difficulty parameters). In the
two-parameter model of Cursio et al. (2019), the measurement model
includes occasion-specific loadings and intercepts (discrimination and
difficulty parameters, respectively). The equivalent multilevel
specification includes cross-level interactions between the latent
missingness propensity and the dummy codes, allowing a person's
propensity to have occasion-specific effects.

The sections below give the algebraic relationships between the two
frameworks, then fit each model to the intensive longitudinal data set
with intermittent missingness (*T* = 20 occasions, *N* = 125) and
compare the `rblimp` output.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Algebraic Relationships

## Notation

Let $m_{ti}$ be the binary missing data indicator for person $i$ at
occasion $t$ ($t = 0, \ldots, T-1$), equal to 1 if the outcome is
missing and 0 otherwise. Blimp estimates binary outcome models on the
latent response metric, so each model below is written for the latent
response variable $m^*_{ti}$ with a standard normal residual (a probit
link):

$$
m_{ti} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } m^*_{ti} > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } m^*_{ti} \le 0 \end{cases}
\qquad \epsilon_{ti} \sim N(0, 1).
$$

The equivalences hold for any link function; only the metric of the
coefficients changes. Let $D_{ti}$ denote the dummy code for occasion
$t$ (equal to 1 if the observation is from occasion $t$ and 0
otherwise), with occasion 0 serving as the reference.

## Dummy-Coded Missingness Model

The dummy-coded missingness model from the paper, with group effects
removed, is a random intercept model with occasion-specific fixed
effects:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \gamma_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t D_{ti} + u_i + \epsilon_{ti},
\qquad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2).
\tag{1}
$$

Because exactly one dummy code is nonzero at each occasion, the model
reduces to a separate intercept for each occasion plus a common random
effect:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \underbrace{(\gamma_0 + \gamma_t)}_{\text{occasion } t \text{ intercept}} + u_i + \epsilon_{ti},
$$

with $\gamma_0$ alone at the reference occasion. The random intercept
$u_i$ is the person-level missingness propensity, and its variance
$\tau^2$ captures stable between-person differences in the tendency to
have missing data. The model has $T$ fixed intercepts and one variance,
for $T + 1$ free parameters.

## One-Parameter IRT Model

The one-parameter (1PL) IRT missingness model treats the $T$ indicators
as items measuring a standardized latent propensity $\eta_i$:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \nu_t + \lambda \, \eta_i + \epsilon_{ti},
\qquad \eta_i \sim N(0, 1).
\tag{2}
$$

Each item has its own intercept $\nu_t$ (the difficulty parameter,
possibly with a sign change depending on the parameterization), and all
items share a common loading $\lambda$ (the discrimination parameter).
The model has $T$ intercepts and one loading, for $T + 1$ free
parameters.

Equations 1 and 2 are the same model. Writing the random intercept as a
scaled standard normal variable, $u_i = \tau \eta_i$, gives the mapping:

| Dummy-Coded Model (Eq. 1) | 1PL IRT Model (Eq. 2) | Relationship |
|:--------------------------|:----------------------|:-------------|
| Reference intercept $\gamma_0$ | Item intercept $\nu_0$ | $\nu_0 = \gamma_0$ |
| Dummy code coefficient $\gamma_t$ | Item intercept $\nu_t$ | $\nu_t = \gamma_0 + \gamma_t$ |
| Random intercept variance $\tau^2$ | Common loading $\lambda$ | $\lambda = \tau$, i.e., $\lambda^2 = \tau^2$ |
| Random intercept $u_i$ | Latent propensity $\eta_i$ | $\eta_i = u_i / \tau$ |

The only difference is where the scale of the latent variable lives: the
dummy-coded model fixes the loading to 1 and estimates the variance,
whereas the IRT model fixes the variance to 1 and estimates the loading.
Both choices identify the same model, and the fit statistics are
identical.

## Multiple-Group Extension

Adding a binary grouping variable $G_i$ and its interactions with the
dummy codes to Equation 1 gives the dummy-coded model with group
effects:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \gamma_0 + \gamma_G G_i + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t D_{ti}
 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_{tG} D_{ti} G_i + u_i + \epsilon_{ti},
\qquad u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2).
\tag{3}
$$

In IRT terms, this is a two-group measurement model in which the item
intercepts differ by group,

$$
\nu_t^{(0)} = \gamma_0 + \gamma_t, \qquad
\nu_t^{(1)} = (\gamma_0 + \gamma_G) + (\gamma_t + \gamma_{tG}),
$$

but the loading $\lambda = \tau$ is common to both groups because the
random intercept variance is the same in both groups. That combination
is metric invariance (equal discriminations) with scalar noninvariance
(group-specific difficulties). Allowing $\tau^2$ to differ by group
would relax metric invariance.

## Two-Parameter IRT Model

The two-parameter (2PL) IRT missingness model adds occasion-specific
loadings:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \nu_t + \lambda_t \, \eta_i + \epsilon_{ti},
\qquad \eta_i \sim N(0, 1).
\tag{4}
$$

Each occasion now has its own discrimination $\lambda_t$, so a person's
missingness propensity can have a stronger or weaker effect at some
occasions than at others. The model has $T$ intercepts and $T$
loadings, for $2T$ free parameters.

The equivalent multilevel specification adds cross-level interactions
between the latent propensity and the dummy codes:

$$
m^*_{ti} = \gamma_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t D_{ti}
 + \lambda_0 \, \eta_i + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \delta_t D_{ti} \, \eta_i + \epsilon_{ti},
\qquad \eta_i \sim N(0, 1).
\tag{5}
$$

The main effect $\lambda_0$ is the loading at the reference occasion,
and each interaction coefficient $\delta_t$ is the change in the loading
at occasion $t$:

| Multilevel Specification (Eq. 5) | 2PL IRT Model (Eq. 4) | Relationship |
|:---------------------------------|:----------------------|:-------------|
| Reference intercept $\gamma_0$ | Item intercept $\nu_0$ | $\nu_0 = \gamma_0$ |
| Dummy code coefficient $\gamma_t$ | Item intercept $\nu_t$ | $\nu_t = \gamma_0 + \gamma_t$ |
| Main effect of $\eta_i$, $\lambda_0$ | Loading $\lambda_0$ | $\lambda_0 = \lambda_0$ |
| Cross-level interaction $\delta_t$ | Loading $\lambda_t$ | $\lambda_t = \lambda_0 + \delta_t$ |

The 1PL model is nested within the 2PL model: setting every $\delta_t$
to 0 in Equation 5 recovers Equation 2. Comparing the two models
therefore tests whether occasion-specific discriminations are needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# rblimp Analyses

## Setup

```{r packages}
library(rblimp)
```

```{r load-data}
filepath <- 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/blimp-stats/mnar-mlm/main/data/intensive-intermittent.csv'

intensive_intermittent <- read.csv(filepath, stringsAsFactors = T)
```

Only the missingness model is specified in each analysis; there is no
focal model. Group effects are omitted so that the dummy-coded model is
fully equivalent to the 1PL model. The `dropout` argument with the
`(missing)` keyword creates the missingness indicator `m`, and
`timeid` identifies the occasion variable. Because `time` is coded 0 to
19, the looping structure `{ t in 1:19 }` generates the dummy codes for
occasions 1 through 19, with occasion 0 as the reference.

## Model A: Dummy-Coded Missingness Model

Model A is the dummy-coded missingness model in Equation 1. The random
intercept after the vertical pipe is the person-level missingness
propensity $u_i$.

*Important features of the missingness model:*

- Boolean statements create dummy codes as functions of the TIME
  variable, such that each condition in parentheses returns 1 if
  TIME = `t` and 0 otherwise.
- A looping structure avoids specifying a separate Boolean statement
  for each occasion.
- The random intercept after the vertical pipe is Blimp's default for a
  multilevel model and could be omitted; it is shown explicitly here
  because the IRT models below fix it to zero.

```{r model-dummy, cache=TRUE}
model_dummy <- rblimp(
  data = intensive_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  fixed = 'time',
  model = '
    m ~ intercept | intercept;
    { t in 1:19 } : m ~ (time == [t]);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model_dummy)
```

## Model B: One-Parameter IRT Model

Model B is the 1PL model in Equation 2. A standardized latent variable
`u` replaces the random intercept, a single common loading on `u` is
estimated, and the occasion dummy codes give the item intercepts.

*Important features of the missingness model:*

- The `latent` argument declares `u` as a level-2 latent variable.
- The structural model fixes the latent variable's mean to 0
  (`u ~ intercept@0`) and its variance to 1 (`u ~~ u@1`).
- The common loading is the coefficient for `u` in the measurement
  model.
- The default random intercept for `m` is fixed to 0 (`| intercept@0`)
  because `u` is the only source of between-person variation.

```{r model-1pl, cache=TRUE}
model_1pl <- rblimp(
  data = intensive_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = u',
  fixed = 'time',
  model = '
    structural:
    u ~ intercept@0;
    u ~~ u@1;
    measurement:
    m ~ intercept u | intercept@0;
    { t in 1:19 } : m ~ (time == [t]);',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 25000,
  iter = 25000)

output(model_1pl)
```

## Model C: Two-Parameter IRT Model

Model C is the 2PL model in Equation 5. The main effect of `u` is the
loading at occasion 0, and the cross-level interactions between `u` and
the dummy codes give the change in the loading at each subsequent
occasion.

*Important features of the missingness model:*

- The structural model fixes the latent variable's mean to 0 and its
  variance to 1, as in Model B.
- The looping structure adds both the dummy code and its product with
  `u` at each occasion; the product terms are the cross-level
  interactions in Equation 5.

```{r model-2pl, cache=TRUE}
model_2pl <- rblimp(
  data = intensive_intermittent,
  clusterid = 'l2id',
  timeid = 'time',
  dropout = 'm = y (missing)',
  latent = 'l2id = u',
  fixed = 'time',
  model = '
    structural:
    u ~ intercept@0;
    u ~~ u@1;
    measurement:
    m ~ intercept u | intercept@0;
    { t in 1:19 } : m ~ (time == [t]) (time == [t])*u;',
  seed = 90291,
  burn = 50000,
  iter = 50000)

output(model_2pl)
```
